summary: Selma sits on the dead-flat floor of the San Joaquin Valley, roughly sixteen miles south of Fresno, surrounded by vineyards, orchards, and packing operations that stretch to the horizon in every direction — and it once branded itself the "Raisin Capital of the World," a nod to the grape-drying industry that still shapes the local economy. That agricultural backbone means jobs in packing, cold storage, and logistics cluster along the Highway 99 corridor that bisects the city, while Fresno's hospitals, distribution centers, and government offices absorb much of the commuting workforce via a straightforward twenty-minute drive north. At a median home value of roughly $289,000 against a median household income near $56,000 — a price-to-income ratio just above 5:1 — buying is strained but not impossible compared to coastal California, though a poverty rate near 20% signals that gap bites hard for many households. Summers are genuinely hot, with average highs pushing well above 90°F from June through September under nearly ten hours of daily sunshine, while winter mornings bring the Valley's signature tule fog, dense enough to slow 99 to a crawl. The compact 5.9-square-mile footprint keeps most errands short, but the street grid is oriented around car travel, with limited trail infrastructure and a downtown that reads more as a service corridor than a walkable core. Selma is a small, affordable, agriculture-driven city where proximity to Fresno does the heavy lifting for amenities, and the Central Valley's extremes of heat and fog define the rhythm of the year.
